qc.label_under_test: A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the speaker or the listener: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me, us or you (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders, and he calls you a snob); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us'/'you'. 'You' fires when you did the first labelling (you treat them as family, and they treat you as staff); after 'I see him as...', a second clause casting you stays weak. The same second clause aimed at him, her or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me or you with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.

neighbours.label: A second labelling clause that turns the label around: after one clause labels a person (sees, treats, calls or considers someone as something), a following clause has someone label either the first labeller in return (two named people or he/she swapping roles) or me, us or you; it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after that second object, most strongly with 'sees/treats someone as' and when a sentence of setting comes first. Weak: a second clause that labels a third person or the same person again, a one-way label with no earlier labelling clause, a return label where I am the one labelling back, a return gesture with no labelling verb, and group nouns (the rebels, the king) swapping roles.
fire: The office was quiet that morning. Maria saw Tom as a rival, and Tom saw Maria as a threat.
It rained all week at the camp. He treated her as a child, and she treated him as a tyrant.
The new teacher considered the boy a troublemaker, while the boy considered the teacher a bully.
At the dinner party, Anna called James a snob, and James called Anna a gossip in return.
The village was small and everyone talked. She sees me as a stranger, and her mother sees me as a thief.
After the long trial, the judge treated the witness as a liar, and the witness treated him as a fool.
My sister sees her coach as a mentor, but the coach sees us as a nuisance.
The house on the hill had been empty for years. He regarded her as an intruder, and she regarded him as a ghost.
quiet: The office was quiet that morning. Maria saw Tom as a rival, and Tom saw his brother as a threat.
It rained all week at the camp. He treated her as a child, and she quietly walked out of the tent.
The new teacher considered the boy a troublemaker and sent him to the principal's office.
At the dinner party, Anna called James a snob, and then she called him a liar too.
The village was small and everyone talked. I see her as a stranger, and I see her mother as a thief.
After the long trial, the judge treated the witness as a liar, and the witness simply bowed his head.
My sister sees her coach as a mentor and visits him every summer.
The house on the hill had been empty for years. He regarded her as an intruder, and I regarded him as a ghost.

predictions: Swapped-role name and he/she pairs fire at or above 0.20; non-swapped second clauses and one-way labels stay low.
